summary_html: The child is **removed from the home** and placed in foster care under court order or emergency authority. Federal statutes tie funding to safety findings, judicial oversight, and permanency planning.

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court held that a juvenile court exceeds its jurisdiction if it transfers legal custody of a child from a parent to the county department at a pre-adjudicatory shelter hearing; at that stage the court may only continue shelter or release the child, and a temporary protective custody order reaches physical custody only.
key_cases.relevance: Foster placement pending adjudication is a placement order only; legal custody may be vested elsewhere only after an adjudication under section 19-3-111.
key_cases.quote: We will not infer from statutory silence a jurisdictional grant to a juvenile court to sever legal custody from a natural parent at a pre-adjudicatory shelter hearing.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit adopted a reasonable-suspicion standard for warrantless emergency removal, holding that officials may remove a child without prior notice and hearing only on reasonable suspicion of an immediate threat to the child's safety and must then provide a prompt post-removal hearing, and found the defendants entitled to qualified immunity on these facts.
key_cases.relevance: A placement made on emergency authority must be promptly ratified in a post-removal hearing before it can continue.
key_cases.quote: even in these instances in which emergency removal is justified, the state must afford the parents a prompt post-removal hearing.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Tenth Circuit reversed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that the plaintiff had not shown clearly established law creating a special relationship between himself and the Colorado adoption-exchange officials who arranged his out-of-state placement, and declined to decide whether the special-relationship doctrine can cross state lines.
key_cases.relevance: Once the state takes custody and places a child, the special-relationship doctrine is the source of the state's affirmative constitutional duty to protect that child.
key_cases.quote: First, the plaintiff must demonstrate the existence of a special relationship, meaning that the plaintiff completely depended on the state to satisfy basic human needs.

key_cases.holding: The court held that foster parents who satisfy the criteria of section 19-3-507(5)(a) may intervene and participate fully as parties at a termination hearing, and that parents' due process rights are not impaired by that full participation.
key_cases.relevance: Once a child has been in a foster home for more than three months, the foster parents acquire a statutory right to intervene as parties, which changes the litigation posture of the placement.
key_cases.quote: Foster parent intervenors are afforded the same degree of participation as all other parties, and such participation is not limited to the dispositional hearing.

common_failures: Failure to consider less restrictive alternatives

timeline_requirements.deadline: 72 hours, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and court holidays
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Temporary custody placed with the county department, or an emergency protection order entered

citation.citation_text: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 19-3-403(3.5) (C.R.S. 2024) — when temporary custody is placed with the county department or an emergency protection order is entered, the court holds a hearing within seventy-two hours, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and court holidays

timeline_requirements.deadline: Within a reasonable period set by the title IV-E agency, and in no event later than 60 days
timeline_requirements.starts_from: The child's removal from the home

citation.citation_text: 45 C.F.R. § 1356.21(g)(2) (federal title IV-E case plan requirements)

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Shelter or temporary holding facility hearing
timeline_requirements.deadline: 48 hours, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Law enforcement places the child in a court-designated shelter or temporary holding facility

citation.citation_text: Colo. Rev. Stat. § 19-3-403(2) (C.R.S. 2024) — when law enforcement places the child in a court-designated shelter or temporary holding facility, the court holds the hearing within forty-eight hours, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays

notice_requirements.timing: Once the court knows or has reason to know the child is an Indian child, the petitioning or filing party sends notice by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, to the parents, any Indian custodian, and the tribal agent designated in 25 CFR 23; the postal receipts must be attached to the complaint, petition, or other commencing pleading
